title: A Wardrobe for the Silence
premise: Jonah Kavanagh, once a celebrated composition prodigy, returns to the conservatory where their career ended—not as a composer but as a night janitor, cataloguing silences the way they once catalogued notes. When a radio broadcast airs a song Jonah wrote at fifteen and never recorded, it becomes clear someone in the family has been keeping more than memories alive. As demolition of the old rehearsal wing approaches, Jonah must confront the truth of what happened the night their sister Vera's career was sacrificed to save theirs, and decide whether justice means confession, restitution, or simply saying the unsaid aloud. The book ends with Jonah performing the song publicly on the eve of demolition, giving authorship back to Vera and finally belonging—to the family, to the music, to themselves.
about_author: Silas Winterbourne is the pen name of a former conservatory custodian who spent eleven years sweeping concert halls before publishing a debut story collection praised for its 'tender attention to people the spotlight forgets.' They live near a decommissioned music school and write exclusively at night.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. Twenty years after fleeing the conservatory in disgrace, Jonah takes a night janitorial job there, methodically cleaning the rehearsal rooms where they once performed. The emotional beat is guarded numbness—Jonah treats mopping as penance and keeps a mental ledger of everything the family never discussed, establishing the silence as both shield and prison.

chapters.title: The Song on Frequency 91.3
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. Driving home at dawn, Jonah hears a local station play an untitled piano piece—their own adolescent composition, one that was never recorded or published. Shaken, they begin investigating who could have preserved it. The beat is vertigo: the past has breached the walls Jonah built, and invisibility suddenly feels like a choice someone else made for them.

chapters.title: Vera's Hands
chapters.summary: POV: alternating Jonah and flashbacks from Vera's perspective. Flashbacks show teenage Vera practicing until her hands bled while teachers fawned over Jonah's effortless gift. In the present, Jonah visits their mother, who deflects with pleasantries. The beat is quiet dread—readers begin sensing the family arranged itself around a sacrifice no one will name.

chapters.title: Demolition Notices
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. The conservatory announces the old rehearsal wing will be demolished in six weeks; a preservationist archivist, Noor, is cataloguing its contents. Jonah recognizes the wing as the site of the pivotal night. The beat is urgency colliding with avoidance—a literal deadline now hangs over the metaphorical one.

chapters.title: What the Piano Remembered
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah, with Noor emerging as secondary presence. Helping Noor inventory instruments, Jonah finds the rehearsal-wing piano—the one present on the terrible night—and inside its bench, sheet music annotated in two hands: theirs and Vera's. The beat is trembling intimacy; the evidence of shared creation contradicts the family's official story.

chapters.title: The Arrangement
chapters.summary: POV: extended flashback, Vera's POV. The central secret surfaces: the night of the scholarship jury, Vera's performance was sabotaged by their father so that only Jonah would advance, securing the family's finances and his ambitions. Vera agreed to silence in exchange for being sent away. The beat is devastating clarity—justice outside the law begins here, in a living room contract signed with complicity.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Kitchen Table
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. Jonah confronts their father, now diminished by stroke, and their mother, who admits she knew. The father cannot apologize; the mother asks Jonah not to 'upset the balance.' The beat is furious grief—Jonah realizes the whole family's architecture of belonging was built on Vera's erasure, and that staying invisible makes them complicit still.

chapters.title: Noor's Question
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah. Noor, having pieced together Jonah's identity from the manuscript, asks plainly: whose song is it? Jonah lies, then can't sleep, then returns and tells the truth. Noor proposes broadcasting the piece's true provenance before demolition. The beat is fragile hope—an outsider offers what family never did: witness without conditions.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Machines
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah, climax. At the conservatory's farewell concert, Jonah walks onstage uninvited, reveals themselves as the janitor who was once the prodigy, and performs the song—announcing it as co-written with Vera Kavanagh, whose career was stolen. The room holds its breath; the father watches from the back. The beat is cathartic exposure: the silence finally broken in the exact hall where it was manufactured.

chapters.title: A Wardrobe for the Silence
chapters.summary: POV: Jonah, resolution. Aftermath: the recording circulates, credited properly; Vera calls for the first time in years, and they speak about ordinary things, which feels like grace. Watching the wrecking ball take the wing, Jonah keeps the bench-sheet music and a single key. The beat is earned peace—belonging rebuilt not on silence, but on what was finally said.
